claim: The centromere parS is the first DNA locus to be segregated following chromosome replication.
source: The centromere parS is the first DNA locus to be segregated following chromosome replication (Lin and Grossman, 1998; Livny et al., 2007; Toro et al., 2008; Lagage et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: ParB specifically nucleates on parS before spreading outwards to the flanking DNA.
source: ParB specifically nucleates on parS before spreading outwards to the flanking DNA and bridges/cages DNA together to form a nucleoprotein network in vivo (Breier and Grossman, 2007; Murray et al., 2006; Taylor et al., 2015; Graham et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2015; Debaugny et al., 2018; Broedersz et al., 2014; Funnell, 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: ParB bridges/cages DNA together to form a nucleoprotein network in vivo.
source: ParB specifically nucleates on parS before spreading outwards to the flanking DNA and bridges/cages DNA together to form a nucleoprotein network in vivo (Breier and Grossman, 2007; Murray et al., 2006; Taylor et al., 2015; Graham et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2015; Debaugny et al., 2018; Broedersz et al., 2014; Funnell, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: The ParB nucleoprotein complex recruits SMC to disentangle and organize replicated DNA.
source: This nucleoprotein complex recruits SMC to disentangle and organize replicated DNA (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Sullivan et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2017; Tran et al., 2017; Minnen et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: ParB-parS interacts with an ATPase ParA to power the segregation of replicated chromosomes.
source: ParB-parS also interacts with an ATPase ParA to power the segregation of replicated chromosomes (Lim et al., 2014; Vecchiarelli et al., 2014; Vecchiarelli et al., 2012; Hwang et al., 2013; Leonard et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Engineered strains harboring a nucleation-competent but spreading-defective mutant of parB are either unviable or have elevated number of anucleate cells.
source: Engineered strains harboring a nucleation-competent but spreading-defective mutant of parB are either unviable (Mohl et al., 2001) or have elevated number of anucleate cells (Harms et al., 2013; Kawalek et al., 2018; Lin and Grossman, 1998; Lagage et al., 2016; Jecz et al., 2015; Attaiech et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2010; Lee and Grossman, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: ParB spreading has been observed in vivo by chromatin immunoprecipitation in multiple bacterial species since 1995.
source: Since the first report in 1995 (Lynch and Wang, 1995), ParB spreading has been observed in vivo by chromatin immunoprecipitation in multiple bacterial species (Tran et al., 2018; Lagage et al., 2016; Breier and Grossman, 2007; Murray et al., 2006; Graham et al., 2014; Rodionov et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The nucleation of ParB on parS has been demonstrated in vitro.
source: The nucleation of ParB on parS has also been demonstrated in vitro (Harms et al., 2013; Mohl et al., 2001; Breier and Grossman, 2007; Murray et al., 2006; Sanchez et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Surtees and Funnell, 2001; Ah-Seng et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: parS-dependent ParB spreading has resisted biochemical reconstitution prior to this work.
source: however, parS-dependent ParB spreading has resisted biochemical reconstitution (Taylor et al., 2015; Graham et al., 2014; Fisher et al., 2017; Madariaga-Marcos et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Bacillus subtilis and Myxococcus xanthus ParB bind and hydrolyze CTP to CDP.
source: Recently, works by Soh et al. (2019) and Osorio-Valeriano et al. (2019) on Bacillus subtilis and Myxococcus xanthus ParB, respectively, showed that ParB binds and hydrolyzes cytidine triphosphate (CTP) to cytidine diphosphate (CDP)
evidence: Supported by citations to recent published work

claim: CTP modulates the binding affinity of ParB to parS.
source: and that CTP modulates the binding affinity of ParB to parS (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: CTP binding promotes a new dimerization interface between N-terminal domains of ParB subunits.
source: A co-crystal structure of Bacillus ParB with CDP and that of a Myxococcus ParB-like protein (PadC) with CTP showed CTP binding promotes a new dimerization interface between N-terminal domains of ParB subunits (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies

claim: Bacillus ParB, in the presence of CTP, forms a self-loading protein clamp at parS and slides away to spread to neighboring DNA.
source: Crucially, Soh et al. (2019) showed by single-molecule imaging and cross-linking assays that Bacillus ParB, in the presence of CTP, forms a self-loading protein clamp at parS and slides away to spread to neighboring DNA (Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published single-molecule imaging and cross-linking studies

claim: Caulobacter crescentus ParA-ATP dissociated pre-bound ParB from parS.
source: While reproducing a key result from Easter and Gober (2002) that showed Caulobacter crescentus ParA-ATP dissociated pre-bound ParB from parS (Easter and Gober, 2002), we found that CTP could also modulate the nucleation of Caulobacter ParB on parS.
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: CTP modulates the nucleation of Caulobacter ParB on parS.
source: While reproducing a key result from Easter and Gober (2002) that showed Caulobacter crescentus ParA-ATP dissociated pre-bound ParB from parS (Easter and Gober, 2002), we found that CTP could also modulate the nucleation of Caulobacter ParB on parS.
evidence: Supported by experimental findings in the manuscript

claim: This work reconstitutes a parS-dependent ParB spreading on DNA in real-time using purified proteins from Caulobacter crescentus.
source: Here, we reconstitute a parS-dependent ParB spreading on DNA in real-time, using a label-free purified protein from Caulobacter crescentus.
evidence: Describes the experimental approach and findings of the manuscript

claim: CTP is required for Caulobacter ParB spreading.
source: Consistent with pioneering works by Soh et al. (2019) and Osorio-Valeriano et al. (2019), we confirm that CTP regulates ParB-DNA interaction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in the manuscript and citations to related work

claim: ParB spreading requires a closed DNA substrate.
source: We further provide evidence that the accumulation of Caulobacter ParB requires a closed DNA substrate
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Caulobacter ParB bound site-specifically to parS but not to non-cognate DNA.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Tran et al., 2018; Figge et al., 2003), Caulobacter ParB bound site-specifically to parS but not to non-cognate DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous reports

claim: In the presence of ATP, GTP, or UTP, a small reduction in ParB-parS binding at steady state was observed regardless of whether Mg2+ was included.
source: In the presence of ATP, GTP, or UTP, we observed a small reduction in ParB-parS binding at steady state regardless of whether Mg2+ was included in binding buffer or not (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: CTP had a pronounced effect on ParB-parS interaction, specifically in the presence of Mg2+.
source: However, we noted that CTP had a pronounced effect on ParB-parS interaction, specifically in the presence of Mg2+ (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: An increasing concentration of CTP (but not CMP or CDP) gradually reduced the binding of ParB to parS.
source: An increasing concentration of CTP (but not CMP or CDP) gradually reduced the binding of ParB to parS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Neither CTP nor other NTPs affected the binding of TetR to tetO.
source: In contrast, neither CTP nor other NTPs affected the binding of another protein-DNA pair, for example, the well-characterized TetR-tetO interaction (Saenger et al., 2000; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and citation to published work on TetR-tetO

claim: ParB + CTP slowly dissociated from parS even before the probe was returned to a protein-free buffer.
source: On closer inspection, we noted that ParB + CTP slowly dissociated from parS even before the probe was returned to a protein-free buffer (a gradual downward slope between 30th and 150th sec, Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: ParB dissociated approximately seven times faster in buffer with CTP than in buffer only solution.
source: we found ParB dissociating ~seven times faster in buffer with CTP than in buffer only solution (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: CTP might decrease ParB nucleation on parS or liberates pre-bound ParB from parS site.
source: Given the short length of a 20 bp parS DNA duplex that has only sufficient room for nucleation, our results suggest that CTP might decrease ParB nucleation on parS or liberates pre-bound ParB from parS site.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with 20 bp parS DNA

claim: The addition of CTP significantly increased the BLI response by approximately 12 fold with a 169 bp parS probe.
source: However, the addition of CTP significantly increased the response by ~12 fold (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: More ParB associated with a 169 bp parS probe at steady state in the presence of CTP than by nucleation at parS alone.
source: suggesting that more ParB associated with a 169 bp parS probe at steady state than by nucleation at parS alone.
evidence: Inferred from the increased BLI response in the presence of CTP

claim: DNA-bound ParB was salt sensitive and dissociated readily to the solution when the BLI probe was returned to a low-salt protein-free buffer without CTP.
source: We observed that DNA-bound ParB was salt sensitive and dissociated readily to the solution when the BLI probe was returned to a low-salt protein-free buffer without CTP (Figure 2A, dissociation phase).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The dissociation of pre-bound ParB-CTP from DNA was slowed down by approximately fivefold if the probe was returned to a buffer supplemented with CTP.
source: However, the dissociation of pre-bound ParB-CTP from DNA was slowed down by ~fivefold if the probe was returned to a buffer supplemented with CTP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: The effect on the BLI response was not seen if Mg2+ was omitted.
source: The effect on the BLI response was not seen if Mg2+ was omitted (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: No equivalent increase in response was observed when a 169 bp dual biotin-labeled DNA containing a scrambled parS was employed.
source: neither did we observe an equivalent increase in response when a 169 bp dual biotin-labeled DNA containing a scrambled parS was employed instead (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: A nucleation-competent but spreading-defective Caulobacter ParB (R104A) mutant did not respond to the addition of CTP to the same extent as ParB (WT).
source: Furthermore, we observed that a nucleation-competent but spreading-defective Caulobacter ParB (R104A) (Tran et al., 2018) mutant did not respond to the addition of CTP to the same extent as ParB (WT) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citation to published work on the R104A mutant

claim: CTP is required for the increase in parS-dependent ParB accumulation in vitro.
source: Our results suggest that CTP is required for the increase in parS-dependent ParB accumulation in vitro.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with CTP and various controls

claim: The specific effect of CTP on enhancing ParB association with a closed DNA in vitro was consistently observed for eight additional chromosomal ParB proteins from diverse bacterial species.
source: Lastly, we performed BLI experiments for eight additional chromosomal ParB proteins from a diverse set of bacterial species and consistently observed the specific effect of CTP on enhancing ParB association with a closed DNA in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: ParB-CTP interaction with DNA is likely conserved among ParB orthologs.
source: It is most likely that ParB-CTP interaction with DNA is conserved among ParB orthologs.
evidence: Inferred from observations with multiple ParB orthologs from diverse species

claim: Approximately 13-15 fold more ParB was pulled down when CTP was included in the pull-down assay.
source: We found ~13–15 fold more pulled-down ParB when CTP was included (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: No enrichment of ParB was observed when scrambled parS-coated beads were used in the pull-down assay.
source: No enrichment was observed when scrambled parS-coated beads were used, confirming that the extensive in vitro association of ParB with DNA is dependent on parS (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: No further enrichment of ParB was seen when ATP, GTP or UTP was included in the pull-down assay.
source: Also, consistent with the BLI experiments, no further enrichment of ParB was seen when ATP, GTP or UTP was included (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: ParB (R104A) variant was not enriched in the pull-down assay regardless of whether CTP was present or not.
source: Furthermore, a ParB (R104A) variant was not enriched in our pull-down assay regardless of whether CTP was present or not (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: A parS-dependent accumulation of ParB on a closed DNA substrate requires CTP.
source: Altogether, our results suggest that a parS-dependent accumulation of ParB on a closed DNA substrate requires CTP.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations with CTP and closed DNA substrates

claim: An enhanced ParB association with a closed DNA substrate was observed in the presence of CTP before restriction enzyme digestion.
source: Before restriction enzyme digestion, we again observed an enhanced ParB association with a closed DNA substrate in the presence of CTP (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: After digestion by either BamHI or EcoRI, the inclusion of CTP had no effect on the BLI response.
source: After digestion by either BamHI or EcoRI, the inclusion of CTP had no effect on the BLI response, indicating that ParB did not accumulate on an open DNA substrate in vitro (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C

claim: ParB did not accumulate on an open DNA substrate in vitro.
source: After digestion by either BamHI or EcoRI, the inclusion of CTP had no effect on the BLI response, indicating that ParB did not accumulate on an open DNA substrate in vitro (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of BLI response after restriction enzyme digestion

claim: In the presence of BamHI, ParB binding to DNA reduced gradually over 30 min.
source: Here, in the presence of BamHI, ParB binding to DNA reduced gradually over 30 min, while it was unaffected if heat-inactivated BamHI was employed instead (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: ParB-CTP failed to accumulate when a 2.8 kb dual biotin-labeled DNA was linearized by HindIII digestion in the pull-down assay.
source: Lastly, consistent with BLI experiments, our pull-down assay also showed that ParB-CTP failed to accumulate when a 2.8 kb dual biotin-labeled DNA was linearized by HindIII digestion (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: An enhanced ParB association with DNA was observed with a closed 170 bp DNA substrate containing parS and tetO in the presence of CTP.
source: With this closed DNA substrate, we observed an enhanced ParB association with DNA in the presence of CTP (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The addition of ParB + CTP had no effect on the BLI response with a BamHI-restricted 170 bp DNA probe.
source: Consistent with previous experiments with a restricted 169 bp DNA probe, the addition of ParB + CTP had no effect on the BLI response (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: ParB accumulation was partially rescued by incubating a BamHI-restricted DNA probe with a premix of ParB + CTP + TetR.
source: However, it can be partially rescued by incubating a BamHI-restricted DNA probe with a premix of ParB + CTP + TetR (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: TetR binding at tetO capped the open DNA end, essentially generating a closed DNA substrate.
source: We reason that TetR binding at tetO capped the open DNA end, essentially generated a closed DNA substrate.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of ParB accumulation by TetR

claim: No enhanced association of ParB with DNA was observed with an EcoRI-restricted DNA even when TetR was included.
source: Here, we did not observe an enhanced association of ParB with DNA even when TetR was included, most likely because of a persistent open DNA end that could not be blocked by TetR-tetO binding (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: TetR could attenuate ParB-CTP accumulation on a closed DNA substrate.
source: Finally, we observed that the TetR could attenuate ParB-CTP accumulation on a closed DNA substrate (magenta line vs. orange line, Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The blocking effect of TetR is specific to TetR-tetO binding.
source: This blocking effect is specific to TetR-tetO binding since the addition of anhydrotetracycline (ahTc), a negative effector of TetR (Saenger et al., 2000), allowed ParB-CTP to regain its accumulation on DNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to published work on ahTc

claim: The ability of a DNA-bound TetR to act as a roadblock in vitro is consistent with previous ChIP-seq data showing DNA-binding proteins or RNA polymerases could block or attenuate ParB spreading unidirectionally in vivo.
source: Overall, the ability of a DNA-bound TetR to act as a roadblock in vitro is consistent with previous ChIP-seq data that showed DNA-binding proteins or RNA polymerases could block or attenuate ParB spreading unidirectionally in vivo (Breier and Grossman, 2007; Murray et al., 2006; Sanchez et al., 2015; Rodionov et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to published ChIP-seq studies

claim: Caulobacter ParB binds to radiolabeled CTP in the presence of parS DNA.
source: By employing a membrane-spotting assay (DRaCALA), we showed that Caulobacter ParB binds to radiolabeled CTP in the presence of parS DNA (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: An excess of unlabeled CTP, but no other NTPs, could compete with radioactive CTP for binding to Caulobacter ParB.
source: An excess of unlabeled CTP, but no other NTPs, could compete with radioactive CTP for binding to Caulobacter ParB (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Caulobacter ParB does not bind other NTPs.
source: suggesting that Caulobacter ParB does not bind other NTPs.
evidence: Inferred from the competition assay results

claim: The CTP binding of ParB was reduced when a non-cognate DNA site (NBS) was used instead of parS.
source: The CTP binding of ParB was reduced when a non-cognate DNA site (NBS) (Wu and Errington, 2004) was used instead of parS (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citation to published work on NBS

claim: CTP hydrolysis to CDP and inorganic phosphate was robustly detected when Caulobacter ParB and CTP were included, at a rate of approximately 0.4 CTP molecules per ParB per hour.
source: Nevertheless, we robustly detected CTP hydrolysis to CDP and inorganic phosphate when Caulobacter ParB and CTP were included, albeit at a very low rate of ~0.4 CTP molecules per ParB per hour (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: A background level of inorganic phosphate was observed when Caulobacter ParB was incubated with ATP, GTP, or UTP.
source: A background level of inorganic phosphate was observed when Caulobacter ParB was incubated with ATP, GTP, or UTP (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The addition of a 22 bp parS DNA, but not a non-cognate 22 bp NBS DNA, increased CTP turnover rate sevenfold to approximately 3 CTP molecules per ParB per hour.
source: Crucially, the addition of a 22 bp parS DNA, but not a non-cognate 22 bp NBS DNA, increased CTP turnover rate sevenfold to ~3 CTP molecules per ParB per hour (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The CTP hydrolysis was reduced to the background in the nucleation-competent but spreading-defective ParB (R104A) variant.
source: Lastly, the CTP hydrolysis was reduced to the background in the nucleation-competent but spreading-defective ParB (R104A) variant (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: parS DNA stimulates Caulobacter ParB to bind and hydrolyze CTP.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that parS DNA stimulates Caulobacter ParB to bind and hydrolyze CTP.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with parS DNA and CTP binding/hydrolysis

claim: Caulobacter ParB could accumulate on DNA in the presence of CTPγS.
source: We observed that Caulobacter ParB could accumulate on DNA in the presence of CTPγS, but in contrast to when CTP was employed, a longer preincubation time between ParB and CTPγS gradually reduced ParB accumulation on DNA (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: A longer preincubation time between ParB and CTPγS gradually reduced ParB accumulation on DNA.
source: We observed that Caulobacter ParB could accumulate on DNA in the presence of CTPγS, but in contrast to when CTP was employed, a longer preincubation time between ParB and CTPγS gradually reduced ParB accumulation on DNA (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: CTPγS, in the absence of parS DNA, converts apo-ParB in solution to a nucleation-incompetent form over time.
source: Our results suggest the possibility that CTPγS, in the absence of parS DNA, converts apo-ParB in solution to a nucleation-incompetent form over time.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction in ParB accumulation with longer CTPγS preincubation

claim: CTPγS efficiently promoted the engagement between N-terminal domains of Bacillus ParB in the absence of parS DNA.
source: Our observation is reminiscent of a time-course experiment in which CTPγS efficiently promoted the engagement between N-terminal domains of Bacillus ParB in the absence of parS DNA (Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work on Bacillus ParB

claim: The engagement of N-terminal domains converts Bacillus ParB from an open to a closed protein clamp.
source: The engagement of N-terminal domains was shown to convert Bacillus ParB from an open to a closed protein clamp (Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work on Bacillus ParB

claim: The closed form of ParB presumably cannot nucleate/load onto parS due to its now inaccessible DNA-binding domain.
source: If not already bound on DNA, the closed form of ParB presumably cannot nucleate/load onto parS due to its now inaccessible DNA-binding domain (Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from structural understanding and citation to published work

claim: The cross-linking of ParB (Q35C C297S) was enhanced by CTP and CTPγS but not by other NTPs.
source: The cross-linking of ParB (Q35C C297S) was also enhanced by CTP and CTPγS but not by other NTPs, consistent with the specific role of CTP in ParB spreading (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B

claim: CTPγS was twice as efficient as CTP in promoting the cross-linked form between N-terminal domains of Caulobacter ParB.
source: As shown in Figure 6B, CTPγS was twice as efficient as CTP in promoting the cross-linked form between N-terminal domains of Caulobacter ParB.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The rapid increase in the nucleation-incompetent closed form of Caulobacter ParB might explain the overall reduction in accumulation overtime when ParB was preincubated with CTPγS.
source: The rapid increase in the nucleation-incompetent closed form of Caulobacter ParB might explain the overall reduction in accumulation overtime when ParB was preincubated with CTPγS (Figure 6A).
evidence: Inferred from cross-linking and accumulation data

claim: In the presence of CTP, the reaction reached steady state after 120 s and remained stable for the duration of the association phase.
source: In the presence of CTP, the reaction reached steady state after 120 s and remained stable for the duration of the association phase (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: In the presence of CTPγS, ParB accumulation rapidly reached the maximal level after 200 s, then declined slowly over 60 min.
source: However, in the presence of CTPγS, ParB accumulation rapidly reached the maximal level after 200 s, then declined slowly over 60 min.
evidence: Inferred from extended association phase experiments

claim: DNA-bound ParB-CTPγS complexes gradually dissociated from DNA into solution but were not replenished by a new cycle of nucleation-spreading-dissociation.
source: We suggest that DNA-bound ParB-CTPγS complexes gradually dissociated from DNA into solution (possibly via a transient clamp opening or CTPγS leaving its weak binding pocket rather than by hydrolysis) but were not replenished by a new cycle of nucleation-spreading-dissociation because over time most ParB-CTPγS in solution was in a nucleation-incompetent closed form.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with CTPγS over time

claim: CTP hydrolysis is not required for parS-bound ParB to escape the nucleation site to spread.
source: Taken together, we suggest that CTP hydrolysis is not required for parS-bound ParB to escape the nucleation site to spread, but possibly contributes to maintaining the stability of spreading by recycling ParB.
evidence: Inferred from experiments with CTPγS and CTP

claim: CTP hydrolysis possibly contributes to maintaining the stability of spreading by recycling ParB.
source: Taken together, we suggest that CTP hydrolysis is not required for parS-bound ParB to escape the nucleation site to spread, but possibly contributes to maintaining the stability of spreading by recycling ParB.
evidence: Inferred from experiments with CTPγS and CTP

claim: A small molecule (CTP) is required to enable Caulobacter ParB proteins to spread in vitro.
source: In this work, we report that a small molecule (CTP) is required to enable Caulobacter ParB proteins (as well as eight other chromosomal ParB proteins, Figure 2—figure supplement 3) to spread in vitro.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: F-plasmid and P1-plasmid ParB proteins also bind and hydrolyze CTP.
source: Recently, Soh et al. (2019) observed that F-plasmid and P1-plasmid ParB proteins also bind and hydrolyze CTP (Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: The effect of CTP on ParB spreading is likely universal among plasmid and chromosomal ParB orthologs.
source: Hence, it is most likely that the effect of CTP on ParB spreading is universal among plasmid and chromosomal ParB orthologs.
evidence: Inferred from observations with multiple ParB orthologs and citations to published work

claim: A classical mutant ParB (R104A) was not responsive to CTP.
source: A classical mutant whose arginine-rich patch (G101ERRxR) has been mutated to alanine for example ParB (R104A) (Lin and Grossman, 1998) was not responsive to CTP
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to published work on the R104A mutant

claim: CTP is bound to the N-terminal domain of Caulobacter ParB.
source: suggesting that CTP is bound to the N-terminal domain of Caulobacter ParB.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of response in the R104A mutant affecting the N-terminal domain

claim: CDP binds to the arginine-rich patch at the N-terminal domain of Bacillus ParB.
source: Indeed, Soh et al. (2019) reported a co-crystal structure that showed CDP binding to the arginine-rich patch at the N-terminal domain of Bacillus ParB (CTP was hydrolyzed to CDP during crystallization) (Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published structural work

claim: CTP binds to the N-terminal domain of Myxococcus ParB.
source: Osorio-Valeriano et al. (2019) also showed a similar binding pocket of CTP at the N-terminal domain of Myxococcus ParB by hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work using hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry

claim: The N-terminal domain of ParB can oligomerize to bridge DNA together without the need of an additional ligand.
source: Intriguingly, a co-crystal structure of a Helicobacter pylori ParB-parS complex, together with the in vitro magnetic-tweezer and single-molecule TIRF microscopy-based experiments with Bacillus ParB showed that the N-terminal domain can oligomerize to bridge DNA together without the need of an additional ligand (Taylor et al., 2015; Graham et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015; Fisher et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published structural and single-molecule studies

claim: There might be two different modes of action of ParB on DNA: one for bridging DNA together (that does not require CTP) and another for the lateral spreading of ParB on DNA (that requires CTP).
source: There might be two different modes of action of ParB on DNA: one for bridging DNA together (that does not require CTP) and another for the lateral spreading of ParB on DNA (that requires CTP).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on experimental observations and published work

claim: The requirement of a DNA substrate with blocked ends for ParB accumulation in vitro is suggestive of a lateral ParB diffusion along the DNA.
source: The requirement of a DNA substrate with blocked ends for ParB accumulation in vitro is suggestive of a lateral ParB diffusion along the DNA that is ParB can escape by running off a free DNA end (Figure 7).
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with closed vs. open DNA substrates

claim: ParB can escape by running off a free DNA end.
source: The requirement of a DNA substrate with blocked ends for ParB accumulation in vitro is suggestive of a lateral ParB diffusion along the DNA that is ParB can escape by running off a free DNA end (Figure 7).
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with closed vs. open DNA substrates

claim: Inside cells, the spreading and bridging/caging of ParB have been inferred from the compact foci of fluorescently labeled ParB.
source: Inside cells, the spreading and bridging/caging of ParB have been inferred from the compact foci of fluorescently labeled ParB (Harms et al., 2013; Lagage et al., 2016; Sanchez et al., 2015; Thanbichler and Shapiro, 2006; Kusiak et al., 2011; Lin et al., 1997; Glaser et al., 1997; Erdmann et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citations to published fluorescence microscopy studies

claim: Nucleation-competent but spreading-defective ParB mutants formed no or very diffusive foci in vivo.
source: Nucleation-competent but spreading-defective ParB mutants formed no or very diffusive foci in vivo (Graham et al., 2014; Song et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: An artificially engineered double-strand break approximately 8 kb away from parS did not cause a dissolution of ParB foci in Caulobacter cells.
source: Recently, it has been observed that an artificially engineered double-strand break ~8 kb away from parS did not cause a dissolution of ParB foci in Caulobacter cells (Badrinarayanan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: The abundant DNA-bound transcription factors and RNA polymerases in vivo act as roadblocks to minimize ParB runoff.
source: However, we reason that the abundant DNA-bound transcription factors and RNA polymerases in vivo act as roadblocks to minimize ParB runoff.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with TetR and published ChIP-seq data

claim: CTP reduces Caulobacter ParB nucleation at parS.
source: Results from experiments in Figure 1 indicate that CTP modulates ParB nucleation on a parS site.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1

claim: CTP-bound ParB could form a closed protein clamp even in the absence of parS DNA, albeit not energetically favorable.
source: Soh et al. (2019) reported that CTP-bound ParB could form a closed protein clamp even in the absence of parS DNA, albeit not energetically favorable (Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: The DNA-binding domain of a closed ParB clamp would be inaccessible to DNA, especially to a closed DNA substrate.
source: The DNA-binding domain of a closed ParB clamp would be inaccessible to DNA, especially to a closed DNA substrate.
evidence: Inferred from structural understanding of closed ParB clamp

claim: Only apo-ParB or a transiently formed CDP-bound ParB (from CTP hydrolysis) are able to nucleate on parS.
source: It might be that only apo-ParB or a transiently formed CDP-bound ParB (from CTP hydrolysis) are able to nucleate on parS (Figure 7A).
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and structural understanding

claim: Preincubation of Caulobacter ParB with a non-hydrolyzable analog CTPγS promoted efficiently the cross-linked form of ParB and subsequently reduced ParB nucleation and spreading on DNA.
source: Supporting this interpretation, preincubation of Caulobacter ParB with a non-hydrolyzable analog CTPγS promoted efficiently the cross-linked form of ParB and subsequently reduced ParB nucleation and spreading on DNA (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: A weak CTP binding of Bacillus, Caulobacter, and Myxococcus ParBs might be advantageous for the cells as a fraction of intracellular apo-ParB will remain to nucleate on parS.
source: Initially, we were surprised by a weak CTP binding of Bacillus, Caulobacter, and Myxococcus ParBs (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019), however, this might be advantageous for the cells as a fraction of intracellular apo-ParB will remain to nucleate on parS.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on experimental observations and citations

claim: Caulobacter ParB-parS complex binds CTP, and this facilitates ParB dissociation from parS.
source: We showed that Caulobacter ParB-parS complex binds CTP, and this facilitates ParB dissociation from parS (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The DNA-binding domain in Bacillus ParB-CDP co-crystal structure is incompatible with parS binding.
source: It was reported that the DNA-binding domain in Bacillus ParB-CDP co-crystal structure is incompatible with parS binding (Soh et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to published structural work

claim: The incompatibility of the DNA-binding domain with parS binding might enable ParB to escape from a high-affinity nucleation site to non-specific flanking DNA.
source: and this might enable ParB to escape from a high-affinity nucleation site to non-specific flanking DNA.
evidence: Inferred from structural understanding and experimental observations

claim: ParB proteins dissociate off the free end well before the next ParB escapes from the parS nucleation site.
source: Our observation of a low BLI response with an open DNA (Figure 3 and Figure 4) implies that ParB proteins dissociate off the free end well before the next ParB escapes from the parS nucleation site.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with open DNA substrates

claim: The transition from a parS-bound ParB to a spreading ParB might be the rate-limiting step.
source: We suggest that the transition from a parS-bound ParB to a spreading ParB might be the rate-limiting step.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations

claim: Caulobacter ParB diffuses laterally along the DNA.
source: Our observation that Caulobacter ParB did not accumulate on an open DNA suggests that Caulobacter ParB diffuses laterally along the DNA.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with open vs. closed DNA substrates

claim: The ParB-CTP complex forms a sliding clamp that moves along the DNA.
source: Similarly, cross-linking experiments on Bacillus ParB (Soh et al., 2019) proposed that the ParB-CTP complex forms a sliding clamp that moves along the DNA (Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published cross-linking experiments

claim: The diffusive Caulobacter ParB along the DNA is CTP bound.
source: From our experiments with CTPγS (Figure 6) and consistent with Soh et al. (2019), we suggest that the diffusive Caulobacter ParB along the DNA is CTP bound.
evidence: Inferred from experiments with CTPγS and citation to published work

claim: The low CTP hydrolysis rate of Caulobacter ParB (approximately 3 CTP molecules per ParB per hour) while ParB spreading could be observed by BLI within minutes supports the interpretation that the diffusive spreading form of Caulobacter ParB is most likely CTP-bound.
source: The low CTP hydrolysis rate of Caulobacter ParB (~3 CTP molecules per ParB per hour) while ParB spreading could be observed by BLI within minutes also lends support to the interpretation that the diffusive spreading form of Caulobacter ParB is most likely CTP-bound (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: Inferred from CTP hydrolysis rate measurements and BLI observations

claim: For Bacillus and Caulobacter ParB, CTP hydrolysis is not required for ParB to escape from the nucleation site.
source: For Bacillus and Caulobacter ParB, CTP hydrolysis is not required for ParB to escape from the nucleation site (Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to published work

claim: Caulobacter ParB could still spread on a DNA when incubated with a non-hydrolyzable CTPγS, even though spreading was less stable over time in comparison to when CTP was employed.
source: Caulobacter ParB could still spread on a DNA when incubated with a non-hydrolyzable CTPγS (Figure 6), even though spreading, at least in vitro, was less stable over time in comparison to when CTP was employed (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: CTP hydrolysis might contribute to ParB recycling.
source: As suggested for Bacillus ParB (Soh et al., 2019) and supported by our results with Caulobacter ParB, CTP hydrolysis might contribute to ParB recycling instead.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and citation to published work

claim: ParB recycling in vivo is possibly achieved via several routes: (i) CTP dissociation from its weak binding pocket, (ii) CTP hydrolysis, (iii) a possible enhanced CTP dissociation/hydrolysis via collisions with DNA-bound roadblocks, or (iv) a transient clamp opening even when ParB is CTP bound.
source: It is possible that ParB recycling in vivo is achieved via several routes: (i) CTP dissociation from its weak binding pocket, (ii) CTP hydrolysis, (iii) a possible enhanced CTP dissociation/hydrolysis via collisions with DNA-bound roadblocks, or (iv) a transient clamp opening even when ParB is CTP bound.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on experimental observations

claim: The label-free approaches to biochemical reconstitution obviate the often time-consuming and challenging task of site-specifically labeling proteins with fluorophores/chemical crosslinkers without affecting the function of proteins.
source: Beyond the biological significance of the findings, our label-free approaches to biochemical reconstitution obviate the often time-consuming and challenging task of site-specifically labeling proteins with fluorophores/chemical crosslinkers without affecting the function of proteins.
evidence: Based on the methodological approach used in the manuscript

claim: The methodology demonstrated medium-throughput capability by investigating the effect of CTP on the spreading of eight additional chromosomal ParB proteins.
source: Here, we have demonstrated the medium-throughput capability of our methodology by investigating the effect of CTP on the spreading of eight additional chromosomal ParB proteins.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with multiple ParB orthologs

claim: Immobilizing a dual biotin-labeled DNA on a streptavidin-coated BLI probe created a DNA substrate where both ends were blocked (a closed DNA).
source: Immobilizing a dual biotin-labeled DNA on a streptavidin-coated BLI probe created a DNA substrate where both ends were blocked (a closed DNA) (Onn and Koshland, 2011; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental design and citation to published method

claim: Both ParB (C297S) and ParB (Q35C C297S) were competent at spreading in the presence of CTP.
source: Both ParB (C297S) and ParB (Q35C C297S) were competent at spreading in the presence of CTP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A
